instructions: Generate one original concept for a short vertical video whose only goal is to make someone stop scrolling.
The environment is critical: choose a visually interesting setting that adds depth, atmosphere, scale, color, or spectacle.
Every concept must have an immediate visual hook within the first moment of the shot.
Prioritize a clear physical action that progresses visibly across the shot.
Favor novelty and curiosity over jokes: the video does not need to be funny.
Build one escalation into a satisfying or surprising final image.
Keep the premise simple enough to understand within a couple of seconds.
Minimize dialogue, on-screen text, verbal humor, complex narratives, large crowds, and precise multi-step interactions.
The main character should be ALIVE: a person, animal, insect, sea creature, or monster renders most reliably.
creative_directions: Let the environment actively participate: reflections, weather, lighting shifts, crowds, or terrain reacting to the subject.
Use cinematic detail to make the scene feel tangible: textures, depth of field, atmospheric haze, practical light sources.
Contrast scale, color, or mood between subject and background to create visual tension.
Prefer premises that can be summarized as: why does this place look like that, or what is that thing doing?
Use physically filmable wording: name what is visible, what moves, and where the action ends.
Avoid abstract phrasing that cannot be filmed; show concrete objects and visible change.
Keep the prompt to one dominant subject and at most one or two supporting elements.
Use only one transformation or escalation; do not chain multiple events in the same shot.
End with a concrete, memorable final image the video model can clearly render.
Do not force comedy: wonder, beauty, tension, cuteness, and unease are equally valid reactions.
creative_priorities: Immediate visual hook in the first moment.
Strong, visually interesting environment or background.
Escalation or progression across the shot.
diversity_guidance: Rotate emotional registers across concepts: awe, humor, mystery, cuteness, tension, satisfaction.
Do not repeat the same subject type, environment type, or payoff style in consecutive ideas.
Vary shot scale between close-ups and wide establishing shots.
Vary pacing: some concepts slow and atmospheric, others fast and surprising.
wow_factor_guidance: Aim for a reaction in the first seconds: a gasp, a laugh, an aww, a chill, or a how-did-they-do-that.
The final image should be more striking than the setup, never merely louder.
Combine two things nobody combines, or reveal something that recontextualizes the whole frame.
Beauty and satisfaction count as WOW just as much as shock does.
living_subject_rules: The main character must be ALIVE: a person, animal, insect, sea creature, or monster.
Inanimate objects may never be the main character; they can only appear as props, clothing, food, or the absurd element the living character interacts with.
When an object misbehaves, show a living character noticing or reacting to it.
Mutations must stay uncanny and surreal - never gory, bloody, flesh-peeling, organ-exposing, or body-horror graphic.
ltx2_prompt_rules: Write ONE continuous natural-language paragraph in English. No titles, headings, code fences, or markdown.
Start directly with: Style: <visual style>, <rest of the paragraph>. Use the exact visual style given in THIS EPISODE'S VISUAL STYLE.

ESTABLISH THE SHOT: open right after Style with shot scale and framing in cinematic terms the model understands (macro close-up, medium two-shot, low-angle wide, over-the-shoulder, shallow depth of field).
SET THE SCENE: establish the lighting source, color palette, surface textures, and atmosphere as the subject acts.

DEFINE THE CHARACTER: give the living subject recognizable physical traits in one clause - breed or age, size, markings or hair, clothing - and show emotion through visible physical cues, never abstract labels.
DESCRIBE THE ACTION as a natural chronological sequence flowing from setup to payoff, told through what is visibly happening.
CAMERA: include at most one deliberate camera move, described relative to the subject and its effect on the frame. A static locked shot is equally valid when the gag plays better still.
Use active present-progressive verbs (is walking, is opening), not past tense or passive voice.
Maintain strict chronological flow using temporal connectors: as, then, while, when, until.

Describe the complete soundscape inside the same paragraph, integrated chronologically alongside the actions: background music, ambient sounds, and specific sound effects. Name the exact source and texture of every sound, never vague descriptions such as ambient sound is present.

Music must be derived from the concept itself: name the actual mood, tempo, and instruments the absurd situation suggests. Never copy a template of fixed instruments and never reuse a music cue from a previous episode.
Visuals and audio only: do not include smell, taste, or touch.
Do NOT use timestamps, scene cuts, or phrases such as The scene opens with. Start directly with Style.
No dialogue unless speech is essential; if speech is included, put the exact words in quotes with a voice description.
Match detail density to shot scale: close-ups need fine texture and facial detail, wide shots stay simpler.
Be specific but restrained: concrete details such as neon reflections on wet pavement are good; intensifiers such as vibrant, blinding, breathtaking, or massive are not.
The final paragraph is the full prompt that will be fed directly to the video model, so every visual and every sound must be present in this single paragraph.
audio_guidance: Audio (music and sound effects) must be derived dynamically from the concept and escalate together with the action.
EVERY concept must include a named background-music cue woven into the paragraph. Silence or a bare hum is not acceptable.
Name concrete music: identify the actual energy, instruments, or rhythm the scene suggests. Never reuse a fixed template.
Layer sounds chronologically: an establishing ambience, a rising musical cue as the moment builds, and a distinct sound for the payoff.
If the scene implies a hidden-world reveal, include a muffled interior hum or echo; if it implies scale, use deep booms or tinkling miniature sounds.
Keep every sound source referenced to something visible or implied in the scene.

creative_engines: spectacle: scale, color, weather, or light creating instant awe
satisfying motion: perfect loops, transformations, or chain reactions
mystery: something intriguing revealed or half-revealed
cuteness: an adorable subject doing something surprising
gentle absurdity: one impossible thing treated as completely normal
tension and release: anticipation building to a delightful payoff
impossible coexistence of two worlds in one frame
a quiet emotional moment in an extraordinary setting
